compound.title: Compound interest calculator

how.heading: How compound interest works
how.p1: Simple interest is paid only on the money you put in. Compound interest is also paid on the interest you've already earned, so each year the pot that earns interest is a little bigger than the year before.
how.p2: This calculator compounds monthly: each month, a twelfth of the yearly rate is added to the balance, then your deposit goes in. That's close to how most UK savings accounts and investment platforms work, though some pay interest only once a year.
how.formula: With a monthly rate r (yearly rate ÷ 12) and n months, a starting sum P grows to P × (1 + r)ⁿ, and a monthly deposit m grows to m × ((1 + r)ⁿ − 1) ÷ r.

example.heading: An example
example.body: £150 a month for 20 years is £36,000 paid in. At 7% a year, compounded monthly, it grows to about £78,000, so more than half the final pot is interest. At 3% it reaches about £49,000. Time and rate matter more than the size of each deposit.

caveats.heading: What the calculator leaves out
caveats.body: Rates change, and investment returns go down as well as up, so treat the result as an illustration, not a forecast. It ignores tax: interest above your Personal Savings Allowance is taxable unless it sits in an ISA. It also ignores inflation, which shrinks what the final sum will buy.

faq.a1: Interest paid on both the money you put in and the interest it has already earned. Over long periods it makes savings grow faster than the deposits alone.
faq.a2: It depends on the account. This calculator compounds monthly, which is common for UK savings accounts and investments. Yearly compounding gives a slightly lower result at the same rate.
faq.a3: No. Savings rates change and investments can fall in value. Use the result to compare scenarios, not as a promise. Garzoni is education, not financial advice.
